name: Napping / NSDR / yoga nidra
summary: Short naps and guided deep-rest sessions for recovery; naps have decent evidence, yoga nidra is promising but small.
lead: Napping, non-sleep deep rest (NSDR) and yoga nidra are short rest practices used to recover energy or reduce stress. A nap is a short daytime sleep period; yoga nidra is a guided meditation done lying down, often described as between waking and sleeping. NSDR is a more recent label popularised for similar guided-rest protocols; it is not mentioned in Wikipedia's yoga nidra article.

name: Deload weeks / rest days
summary: Planned lighter training weeks and rest days; grounded in periodization theory, little direct deload data.
lead: Deload weeks and rest days are planned reductions in training load, used by lifters and athletes to manage fatigue and recover. A deload is typically a week of reduced volume or intensity; rest days are days without training.

name: Massage / foam rolling / recovery gear
summary: Foam rollers and massage tools for muscle recovery: some short-term mobility benefit in studies, little appearance-specific evidence.
lead: Foam rollers are lightweight cylinders of elastomeric foam that a person places between a muscle and the floor and rolls over using body weight, a practice classed as self-myofascial release. Proponents use them, along with related massage tools, to increase flexibility, reduce soreness and ease muscle knots.

name: Creatine for sleep deprivation
summary: Creatine taken to blunt the cognitive hit of lost sleep: small studies exist, nothing on looks.
lead: Creatine is an organic compound that helps regenerate ATP in muscle and brain tissue and is widely sold as a dietary supplement. Some people in fitness and looksmaxxing circles claim it can offset the cognitive effects of lost sleep.

name: Sleep banking
summary: Sleeping extra ahead of planned sleep loss: studied in military and shift-work settings, with unsettled evidence.
lead: Sleep banking, also called sleep extension, is the practice of sleeping more than usual in the days before an expected period of sleep loss, in the hope of reducing later impairment. It is discussed in military, shift-work and medical contexts and in some self-improvement circles.

name: Sleep to look attractive (beauty sleep research)
summary: The belief that enough sleep makes you look better: visible signs of sleep loss are documented.
lead: The idea of beauty sleep holds that adequate sleep improves how a person looks and that sleep-deprived faces are judged less attractive. It is a staple of appearance advice and looksmaxxing discussion.

name: Eight hours target / 'sleep is looksmaxxing'
summary: Sleep as the baseline looksmax: eight hours is a community target, guidance says 7 to 9 for adults.
lead: The phrase 'sleep is looksmaxxing' expresses the view in appearance communities that adequate sleep is the most basic appearance improvement, often with a target of about eight hours a night.

name: Keto / ketogenic diet
summary: Very low-carb eating for leanness and acne claims: proven for epilepsy, mixed for weight, untested for skin here.
lead: The ketogenic diet is a high-fat, adequate-protein, very low-carbohydrate diet in which the liver produces ketone bodies as fuel. It was developed as a medical therapy for refractory epilepsy, mainly in children. Popularly it is used for weight loss, and some in looksmaxxing communities also use it for leaning out and for acne claims.

name: Low-carb diet
summary: Cutting carbs moderately: slightly faster early weight loss than low-fat diets in trials, with the gap fading over time, and a split of opinion on whether it suits the long term.
lead: A low-carbohydrate diet restricts carbohydrate intake relative to typical Western eating, usually limiting sugars, bread, pasta and starches and relying more on meat, fish, eggs, dairy, nuts and non-starchy vegetables. There is no standard definition: one professional body treats under 20 percent of energy from carbohydrate as low-carb, another uses under 25 percent, and ketogenic variants typically go below about 50 grams a day. This makes studies difficult to compare.
claims: Cutting carbs leaves you tired, hungry and low in libido.
Low-glycaemic carbohydrates are fine; only refined carbs are the problem.
Low-carb diets burn fat more effectively than other diets.
High protein on a low-carb diet protects muscle while cutting.

name: Beef, salt and water diet
summary: The most restrictive carnivore variant, popularised as the lion diet: ruminant meat, salt and water only, with no controlled evidence behind it.
lead: The beef, salt and water diet is the strictest form of the carnivore diet, limiting intake to ruminant meat (mostly beef), salt and water. It is commonly called the lion diet.
claims: Eating only beef, salt and water resolves autoimmune and mood problems.
Humans do not need plant foods.

name: Zero-carb carnivore
summary: Animal foods only and no plants at all: popular online, supported mostly by self-reports, and classed as a fad diet by dietetic bodies.
lead: The carnivore diet, also called the zero-carb diet, is a high-protein, low-carbohydrate regimen in which adherents eat only animal products such as meat, dairy and eggs. Grokipedia describes the strict zero-carb version as the baseline, with no plants and no added carbohydrates, and trace carbohydrates from animal sources generally under 5 grams a day considered acceptable.
claims: No plant foods are needed and plants can be harmful.
Zero-carb carnivore reverses type 2 diabetes and aids weight loss.
High LDL on carnivore is harmless.

name: Ribeye and water carnivore
summary: Strict carnivore eating built around fatty steak and water: a monotony-based protocol with no studies of its own.
lead: Ribeye and water is a shorthand for an extremely narrow carnivore diet built around fatty beef steaks and water. Grokipedia does not describe it as a distinct named protocol, but notes that carnivore advocates recommend fatty cuts such as ribeye, 80/20 ground beef and added tallow so that most calories come from fat rather than protein.

name: Carnivore-ish / animal-based diet
summary: Paul Saladino's meat, organs, fruit, honey and raw dairy approach: a looser carnivore diet with plenty of testimonials and little controlled research.
lead: The animal-based diet emphasises nutrient-dense animal products such as meat, organ meats, fish, eggs and raw dairy, with limited low-toxicity fruits and honey, while excluding vegetables, grains, legumes, nuts and seeds. Wikipedia describes it as a looser variant of the carnivore diet, adding fruit, honey and raw dairy, and credits Paul Saladino with popularising the red-meat-based version.
claims: An animal-based diet is the optimal human diet.
It clears acne and fixes sleep and energy.
The diet failed for some users.
Eating only meat acidifies the body, while vegetables alkalise.

name: Raw egg consumption
summary: Drinking raw eggs for protein and choline, Rocky-style: popular on forums, but health agencies flag Salmonella and research reports lower protein absorption than cooked eggs.
lead: Raw egg consumption means eating or drinking uncooked eggs, commonly blended into shakes. The practice is associated with strength-sports culture, including the image of Rocky Balboa drinking raw eggs, and appears on looksmax.org as a cheap protein and choline source.
claims: Raw eggs are a convenient, nutrient-rich protein source.
Raw eggs have more choline than cooked eggs.
Parasites and bacteria are not a concern.
Raw egg whites cause biotin deficiency.

name: Liver / organ meats (beef liver)
summary: Beef liver is a genuinely nutrient-dense food that forums treat as a skin-and-vitality staple, with no trials on appearance and a documented vitamin A ceiling.
lead: Liver is the organ most often meant by the term organ meats or offal in looksmaxxing and ancestral-diet communities. Beef liver in particular is promoted online as a very concentrated food, rich in preformed vitamin A, vitamin B12, riboflavin, copper and iron, and is described by some forum users as nature's multivitamin .
claims: Beef liver is 'the most powerful food on earth' and outperforms multivitamins.
Raw, unfrozen liver is the best form and cooking or freezing ruins its value.
Eating liver improves skin and general vitality because of its vitamin A and B vitamins.
Vitamin A toxicity from liver is exaggerated.

name: Desiccated organ supplements (beef organs capsules)
summary: Freeze-dried beef liver and organ capsules marketed as a convenient 'nature's multivitamin', with no appearance trials behind them.
lead: Desiccated organ supplements, often sold as beef organ capsules, are dried and encapsulated preparations of animal organs, most commonly beef liver, sometimes combined with heart, kidney, spleen or other tissue. They are promoted in ancestral-diet communities as a convenient substitute for eating organ meats.

name: Bone marrow / bone broth
summary: Slow-simmered bones and marrow, promoted for collagen and skin; popular as a food, with no published trials on appearance.
lead: Bone broth is a cooking liquid made by simmering bones, often with meat scraps, vegetables and herbs, for an extended period. During simmering, collagen in bones and connective tissue turns into gelatin, which thickens the liquid . Bone marrow is the edible tissue inside long bones, found in yellow and red forms, and has been eaten for a very long time .

name: Beef tallow
summary: Rendered beef fat used for frying and, lately, as a face moisturiser; popular online, with no trials on its skin or appearance effects.
lead: Tallow is rendered beef, pork or mutton fat, made mostly of triglycerides. Beef tallow is about 50 percent saturated fat, 42 percent monounsaturated and 4 percent polyunsaturated, with roughly 109 mg of cholesterol per 100 g . It has long been used for frying, soap, candles and lubrication, and fast-food chains including McDonald's fried in tallow-based oil until around 1990 .
claims: Tallow is healthier than seed oils for cooking.
Tallow on skin works as a moisturiser.

name: Tallow skincare
summary: Rubbing rendered beef fat on the face as a moisturiser, popular online with no published trials on tallow itself.
lead: Tallow skincare is the practice of applying rendered beef fat to the skin as a moisturiser, often in the form of a whipped balm. It is an application of beef tallow, a fat historically used in soap and candles .

name: Raw honey / bee pollen
summary: Hive products promoted for skin and testosterone; honey has some wound-care evidence, bee pollen's benefits are described as unproven.
lead: Raw honey is honey taken from the hive and extracted, settled or strained without added heat, so it may retain some pollen and wax particles . Bee pollen is the ball of flower pollen that worker honeybees pack and use as the hive's main food, mixed with nectar and salivary secretions .

name: Fruitarian diet
summary: Eating only fruit for clean skin: no appearance trials exist, and case reports describe nutritional problems.
lead: A fruitarian diet is an eating pattern built primarily or entirely on fruit, sometimes with nuts and seeds, and without animal products. It is more restrictive than veganism or raw veganism, and practitioners differ on what counts as fruit and whether anything else is allowed. In looksmaxxing communities it is sometimes discussed as a route to "clean" skin and leanness.
claims: Eating only fruit gives clear, glowing skin.
A fruit-only diet is a safe long-term way to stay lean.

name: Raw vegan diet
summary: Uncooked plant-only eating: small studies on nutrition, none on looks, and B12 is a recurring concern.
lead: A raw vegan diet consists of uncooked plant foods, typically fruit, vegetables, nuts, seeds and sprouts, usually kept below roughly 40-49 degrees Celsius. It excludes animal products and, in many versions, most cooked or processed foods. It is discussed in appearance communities as a route to better skin, leanness and general health.
claims: Raw vegan eating improves skin and overall health.
Raw diets are risky for children.

name: Vegan diet
summary: Plant-only eating: good data on weight and cardiometabolic markers, nothing on looks, and B12 must be supplemented.
lead: A vegan diet excludes all animal-derived foods, including meat, fish, dairy, eggs and honey. The term was coined by Donald Watson and Dorothy Morgan in November 1944 when the Vegan Society was founded. People in appearance communities discuss it for skin, leanness and even eye colour, though most such claims are anecdotal.
claims: A vegan or raw vegan diet can lighten eye colour.
Veganism causes hair loss or loss of gym gains.
Plant-based eating is healthy for skin and leanness.

name: Vegetarian / pescatarian
summary: Reduced-meat diets with decent population data on health but nothing on looks.
lead: Vegetarian diets exclude meat, and pescatarian diets exclude meat but include fish and seafood; both may include eggs and dairy. The term pescetarian was coined in the UK in the late 1980s and about 3 percent of adults worldwide were estimated to follow this diet in 2017-2018. They are discussed in looksmaxxing contexts as reduced-meat options for skin, leanness and general health.

name: Mediterranean diet
summary: The best-researched diet pattern: strong cardiovascular data, but nothing on looks directly.
lead: The Mediterranean diet is a traditional eating pattern of countries such as Greece, southern Italy and Spain. It emphasises vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes, nuts and extra-virgin olive oil, with moderate fish, poultry, eggs and dairy, low to moderate wine with meals, and limited red meat and sweets. Researcher Ancel Keys popularised the idea after the Seven Countries Study.

name: Anti-inflammatory diet
summary: Whole-food, low-processed eating aimed at inflammation: research targets disease markers, not puffiness or acne.
lead: An anti-inflammatory diet is an eating pattern intended to lower chronic low-grade inflammation by emphasising whole foods rich in omega-3 fatty acids, polyphenols and fibre, while limiting processed foods, refined carbohydrates, added sugars and red and processed meat. The Mediterranean diet is commonly given as a model. In appearance communities it is cited for reducing puffiness and acne.
claims: Cutting processed food reduces facial puffiness and acne.

name: Dairy-free for skin
summary: Cutting milk to clear acne and puffiness: a popular idea backed by weak observational links, not by trials.
lead: Dairy-free for skin is the practice of avoiding milk, and sometimes other dairy products, to reduce acne and, in some online accounts, facial puffiness.

name: No-sugar / sugar-free lifestyle
summary: Avoiding added sugar for clearer, younger-looking skin: health guidelines back less sugar, but skin-specific trials are thin.
lead: A no-sugar or sugar-free lifestyle is an eating pattern that removes or strongly limits added sugars, adopted by some people to improve skin, among other aims.

name: Gluten-free for skin
summary: Going gluten-free for skin: essential for celiac-linked rashes, but no acne trials were found.
lead: Gluten-free for skin refers to avoiding gluten-containing grains in the belief that it improves acne or skin inflammation.

name: Low-sodium for face de-puffing
summary: Cutting salt to slim a puffy face: low sodium lowers blood pressure, but facial effects are unstudied in these sources.
lead: Low-sodium for face de-puffing is the practice of reducing salt intake to lessen perceived facial water retention.
